extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers; readers and critics of literature, theatre, and poetry (coffeehouse audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Short critical essays and coffeehouse reports offering principles for judging and composing stage-characters, dedications, philosophical exposition, and the sublime in poetry. Mixes examples, satire, and prescriptive remarks aimed at authors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage characters as an index of an age's taste
rubrics_metrics.description: "there was no method in the world of knowing the taste of an age, or period of time so good, as by the observations of the persons represented in their comedies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characters presented on the stage (especially in comedies) as evidence of contemporary social manners and taste; cite examples such as Ben Jonson's smoking fop to show how dramatic characters reflect fashions and values of their time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in depiction of women on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare did not show poverty of genius in making his women small in dialogue but drew them "as they then were in life" — women then were mainly mothers, sisters, daughters, and wives, not coquettes or wits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing female characters, represent the social reality of their time and station rather than imposing later fashions; avoid anachronistic notions of female roles. The absence (in that age) of 'shining wits, politicians, virtuosas, free-thinkers' should inform plausible characterization for historical settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal female character (Aspasia) — virtues and naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspasia is presented as "the most exact economist, without appearing busy; the most strictly virtuous, without tasting the praise of it; and shuns applause with as much industry, as others do reproach."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose exemplary female characters by showing modesty, piety, inward virtue, simple manners, and natural dignity; make inward moral qualities visible through unassuming behaviour and a composed mien rather than rhetorical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of the coquette as an anti-pattern (Poluglossa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poluglossa is "acquainted with all the world but herself; who has the appearance of all, and possession of no one virtue... when she speaks of the criminal gratifications of others, that her innocence is only a restraint, with a certain mixture of envy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the coquette as a figure whose talk indexes vice rather than virtue; as an anti-model, emphasise that surface knowledge and showy conversation without inward self-knowledge or genuine virtue undermine character credibility and moral weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panegyric and dedication — avoid mere flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper presents a sample dedication overflowing in exaggerated praise and warns of "the author's general vice" where praise becomes mistaken for flattery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dedications and panegyrics, prefer sincere, measured praise over extravagant, self-serving flattery. Beware dedicating to patrons for transactional gain; such epistles risk being perceived as mercenary and insincere (satirised here by imagining merchants receiving epigrams in exchange for notes). Examples of overblown panegyric are given to show the anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make philosophical exposition lively (use fable and accessible language)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The learned have so long laboured under the imputation of dryness...an ingenious gentleman... resolved to write a system of philosophy in a more lively method, both as to the matter and language... by way of fable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining natural philosophy, use vivacious narrative, allegory, or fable to make abstract or technical material engaging and comprehensible to a wider audience; the page gives the allegorical 'inferior deities' football-turned-worlds as a model of vivid explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Sublime in poetry — natural, fitting, and situation-appropriate similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid "forced and constrained" similes; natural similes arise when the poet, as spectator, relieves imaginative burden by apt metaphor. The highest courage is "to possess itself with tranquillity in imminent danger," best expressed by a fitting image (example: ministering angel in 'The Campaign').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To achieve the sublime: (a) prefer natural, situation-arising metaphors over laborious, strained comparisons; (b) avoid images that honor the brute (e.g., lions, eagles) at the expense of the human subject; (c) choose images that suit both the person and historical moment; (d) use examples that heighten rather than distract from the emotion (the 'ministering angel' simile is praised as both new and fitting). Anti-patterns include similes that feel inanimate (a rock) or simply transfer honour to a brute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as chronicle — combine lyric greatness with documentary memory
rubrics_metrics.description: A great martial poem can be "a chronicle as well as a poem, and will preserve the memory of our hero, when all the edifices and statues...are blended with common dust."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing occasional or celebratory poems (e.g., on military victories), aim to fuse poetic grandeur with accurate, memorable depiction so the poem serves both artistic and historical-preservative functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show inward virtue through outward demeanor (show, don't tell)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Her countenance is the lively picture of her mind, which is the seat of honour, truth, compassion, knowledge, and innocence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey character by making external behaviour, countenance, and manner reflect internal moral and intellectual qualities; let physical demeanour imply interior dispositions instead of relying on explicit moralising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obvious theatrical artifice that cheats the spectator
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of puppet-showmanship: the spectator is cheated by visible wires and trickery ("these thin devices"), and an audience "is grown too wise, and can look through these thin devices.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatrical representations should strive for credible illusion; blatant mechanical tricks or transparent manipulations (e.g., obvious wires on puppets) undermine the audience's suspension of disbelief. Respect the audience's perceptiveness and prefer subtlety in stagecraft.
